name: Compare page
markup: No html in this file. Each variant below carries the path to its own markup at r/compare-page/<variant>.html — fetch the one you need.
description: Several vendors' quotations against one enquiry, side by side, so a buyer can award the order. Line items down, vendors across, rates in the cells and the totals along the bottom — the comparative statement that is attached to the requisition and shown to whoever signs it.
when_to_use: One enquiry, several offers, and a decision that ends with all but one of them dropped. Reach for this when the columns are alternatives rather than records — four vendors against twelve lines, three freight quotes, two revisions of the same vendor's offer — and when what leaves the screen is an award. The neighbour that looks identical is reconcile-page, and the difference is what the two screens are for: reconciliation puts two sets of records that both already exist beside each other and makes them agree, so every difference it draws is an error somebody has to clear and both sides survive the screen; comparison puts alternatives beside each other and picks one, so every difference it draws is a fact about an offer and only one column outlives the screen. If nothing is being chosen, this is the wrong layout. table is wrong for a different reason: a table sorts, and a comparison has no meaningful sort — sorting a matrix by one vendor's column reorders the line items under every other vendor and destroys the thing the reader was reading across, which is why nothing on this page has a sortable header. A register of the quotations themselves — who quoted, when, for how much, still open or expired — is data-table inside index-page, and that is where a quotation is found rather than where it is weighed. One quotation on its own is record-page.
rules: Rows are line items and columns are vendors, and neither axis may be reordered by the reader. A sort control is the first thing somebody asks for and it is the one thing this page must not have: the value of a matrix is that line 7 is line 7 in every column, and a sort applied to one vendor's rates breaks the correspondence the whole screen is made of. Reordering the lines is legitimate only when it is done to the enquiry, before the quotations were sought, and then it is the same order everywhere.

Both axes stick at once, and that is the structural problem of the entry. table/sticky-header pins the head, table/sticky-column pins the first column, and doing both in one scroller costs more than the sum of the two. border-separate border-spacing-0 on the table, because preflight collapses borders onto the table and a collapsed border does not travel with the cell that sticks. Every rule then moves onto the cells, so a 12 by 6 matrix carries the row rule on 72 <td>s instead of on 12 <tr>s. Every sticky cell needs an opaque fill of its own, which means every one of them also stops taking the row hover and has to be given it back with group-hover. And there are two corner cells rather than none: the top-left cell is sticky on both axes and the bottom-left cell is too once the foot sticks, so both need z-20 against z-10 on the three planes around them. The corners are where this ships broken, because a reviewer scrolls one axis at a time and the defect only appears when both are scrolled at once.

The matrix scroller carries position: relative, and it is load-bearing rather than decorative. Every sr-only span on this page — the caption, the words behind an em dash, the reason a cell is excluded — is position: absolute with no positioned ancestor, so its containing block is the document and it reports its static position from the sixth vendor column, six hundred pixels past the right edge of a phone. The scroller clips it out of sight and the page still grows a horizontal scrollbar, which is the one thing this system does not allow. One relative on the scroller fixes every one of them at once, and it is measured at 390px on a page with the sr-only text in it, because with the spans removed the defect disappears and the fix looks unnecessary.

The scroller carries tabindex="0" and a name. A div with overflow-auto is not focusable in Chromium, so a keyboard user cannot pan a matrix that scrolls in two axes at all — the content is on screen, reachable by every other means, and simply unreachable by the arrow keys. Firefox makes scrollable regions focusable and Chrome does not, which is why this passes review on one machine.

L1 per line is arithmetic and the award is not. The lowest rate on a line is a fact the page can compute; who gets the order is decided by freight, duty, the terms of payment, the delivery date, whether the quotation is still valid and whether that vendor has ever delivered on time. A screen that marks the smallest number and stops has told the buyer something true and let them believe it was the answer, so the terms band and the landed figures are not an optional extra region — they are what stops the mark being read as a recommendation.

The L1 mark is a graphite pill and a weight, never a colour behind the cell. Three reasons and none of them is taste. Colour in this system says what a record is doing, and cheapest is not a state; green means finished and borrowing it for lowest spends a colour that meant something. A field of colour behind a figure is what the colour rule forbids outright, whatever the hue. And on a twelve-line matrix there are twelve marks scattered across four columns, so a tinted cell reads as a pattern in the grid rather than as a set of separate decisions, which is exactly the failure the status pill exists to avoid.

Absent is not zero and the total must not pretend otherwise. A vendor who did not quote three lines has a total for nine lines, and that number is smaller than everyone else's for a reason that has nothing to do with price. The foot states the line count under every total, a partial total is excluded from the mark on the total row, and the reason is written where the figure is — not in a footnote under the table, which is below the fold on the screen this decision is actually made on.

GST is shown and is not compared. A registered buyer recovers it as input credit, so a comparison ranked on a figure that includes it ranks on money nobody spends; freight and non-creditable duty are the two that genuinely change the landed cost and therefore the answer. The page carries all three, ranks on basic plus freight plus duty, and labels the tax row as recovered so nobody adds it back by hand.

An alternative make is quoted against the enquiry, not against the other vendors. A rate for a grade nobody asked for is not a lower price for the same thing, and it cannot carry the L1 mark until somebody with the authority to accept the substitution has accepted it. The cell keeps the figure, says what was offered instead, and is excluded from the line mark and from the comparable total.

table-fixed with every column width declared, on every variant. Under auto layout the widest vendor name decides the width of its own column, so four columns of identical figures come out four different widths and the digits stop lining up across the row — which is the one thing a rate matrix is for. Fixed widths also mean the L1 pill appearing in a cell cannot widen the column, so switching the comparison from basic to landed moves the mark without moving a single figure.

Vendor names wrap in the header and are never truncated. A truncated vendor name is a different vendor as far as anyone reading it out is concerned, and the column heading is the one place on this page where the reader has to be certain which offer they are looking at. Rates and totals take whitespace-nowrap for the opposite reason: ₹15,60,370 broken between the symbol and the digits stops being a figure.

Six vendors is the ceiling and it is a width budget, not a preference. A rate column wide enough for ₹1,72,120 and an L1 pill is 176px, the line-item column is 256px, and a sixth vendor puts the matrix at 1,312px — already a sideways scroll on the 1,366px laptops these are worked on. The answer to a seventh quotation is to drop the ones that are out of the running before the comparison, which is a decision a buyer makes anyway, not a narrower column.

The award bar states what it is about to do before it does it, in the units of the record: how many purchase orders, against which vendors, for how much, and whether the L1 offer is being passed over. A split award that raises three orders instead of one is a fact the person signing has to be told on this screen, because the saving that justified it is smaller than it looks once three deliveries and three sets of paperwork are counted.

An award that is not L1 needs a reason and the reason is a field, not a checkbox. This is the internal control the whole screen exists to serve: a comparative statement is filed with the requisition and read by audit a year later, and "lowest not accepted" with nothing after it is what turns a routine file into a question nobody can answer. Guard the button on the field having content, never disable it — a disabled button beside an empty box explains nothing.

The page renders inside app-shell, and its own root here is a bounded preview frame. As a real screen, drop the wrapper's height and border, keep the max-width and the padding, and let the matrix keep its own scroller: the matrix is the one region on this page allowed to scroll sideways, and the page behind it never does.

anatomy.description: The page-header component unchanged: breadcrumb, the one h1 — Comparative statement — the enquiry's status pill, and the actions. Never sticky; the award bar at the foot is what has to stay reachable.

A white strip of the facts every column is quoted against: the enquiry number, what it is for, the plant, how many quotations arrived out of how many were invited, and when the enquiry closed. Without it the columns are four prices for nothing in particular.

The segmented track that chooses the basis of the comparison — basic rate or landed cost. It moves the mark and the emphasis and changes nothing in the cells, so the rates a vendor actually quoted are on screen under either basis.

The div that owns the sideways scroll: overflow-auto, overscroll-contain, tabindex="0" and a name, with a negative focus offset because it sits flush inside a clipped panel. The only region on the page that scrolls in x.
The top-left <th>, sticky on both axes and z-20. It names the row axis — Line item — and it is the cell that is painted over from one side or the other when the layering is wrong.

One <th scope="col"> per quotation: the vendor's name at 13px in sentence case, the quotation number and its date under it. Right-aligned over right-aligned figures, bottom-aligned so the quote references line up when a long name wraps.
A <th scope="row"> carrying the item name, its code and the enquired quantity with its unit. It is the frozen column, so it carries an opaque fill and the row hover has to be put back on it.
The quoted rate per unit on the first line and the extended line value under it in 12px zinc-500. Both tabular-nums, both nowrap, right-aligned so the column reads as a column.

A small graphite pill reading L1 to the left of the figure, with the figure stepped up to zinc-900 and font-semibold while the unmarked cells sit at zinc-600. The key sits under the matrix and says what L1 means on this page.

The rows that are not numbers — payment terms, promised delivery, quotation validity, warranty, past on-time performance, whether there is a live rate contract. Left-aligned in a matrix built for right-aligned figures, and carrying no L1 mark on any row.

A <tfoot> holding the totals, the derived landed rows and the line count under each. A total is never one more row in the body: a partial total in the body reads as a line item and is announced as one.

The strip at the foot of the scrolling column: the shape of the award, what it will raise, the reason field when the award is not L1, and Award beside Cancel. Opaque and top-bordered, like every other action bar in the system.

behaviour: Nothing on this page sorts. The header cells are labels, not buttons, and there is no aria-sort anywhere on the matrix, because a sort applied to one vendor's column reorders the lines under all of them.

The matrix scrolls in both axes inside its own box. The head stays while the lines scroll, the line column stays while the vendors scroll, and where a foot is sticky it stays as well; the page behind the matrix never moves sideways at any width.

The L1 mark is recomputed from the rates on screen, so it cannot disagree with the figures beside it. Two vendors at the same rate are both marked — L1 is a rate, not a rank, and marking the first one in DOM order would make the award look decided by the order the quotations happened to arrive in.

Changing the basis from basic to landed moves the mark and the emphasis and touches nothing else. Every quoted rate stays on screen under both, and the row the mark is sitting in is the one the ranking is being read from.

A vendor who did not quote a line gets an em dash and the words in the accessibility tree; its total is drawn with the number of lines it covers, and it takes no mark on the total row however small the number is.
A line quoted against an alternative make keeps its figure and is excluded from that line's mark. It stays excluded until the substitution is accepted, which is a decision made off this page.

Choosing a whole-order award selects one vendor for every line. Choosing a split award replaces the matrix with one decision per line, and the running total under it is the sum of the choices rather than any vendor's quoted total.

The award bar restates the award in the record's own units on every change — how many orders, to whom, for how much — and says when the L1 offer is being passed over. The reason field appears with that sentence and the button is guarded on it, never disabled.

The matrix keeps its panning box at every width rather than disappearing below md, because a frozen line column and a pannable grid is what makes a narrow desktop window work and there is no card form of a comparison to fall back to. What a phone ships is a different arrangement, not a smaller grid: one vendor at a time, chosen from a select, with that vendor's rate against every line and the L1 rate beside it as the reference, and the totals and the award action on the phone in full.
accessibility: One <main>, one <h1> in the page header, and every region below it an h2 — the matrix, the terms, the award. The heading outline is what lets anybody skim a comparison without reading four columns of figures.

The matrix carries a <caption>, sr-only, naming the enquiry and saying what the rows and the columns are. Without it a screen reader entering the table is told the number of rows and columns and nothing about which axis is which.

Vendor headers are <th scope="col"> and line headers are <th scope="row">, both, without exception. A rate is meaningless without both of its coordinates, and a figure four columns along announced on its own is the failure the two scopes exist to prevent.

The scroller is a role="region" with an accessible name and tabindex="0", so it appears in the tab order and the arrow keys pan it. Chromium does not make an overflow container focusable on its own, so without this the matrix is operable by mouse and by nothing else.

The focus outline on the scroller takes the negative offset — focus-visible:-outline-offset-2 — because it sits flush inside a panel that is overflow-hidden for its rounded corners, and a positive offset draws two thirds of an outline with the sides clipped away.
A cell nobody quoted is an em dash for the eye and the words "Not quoted" in an sr-only span. An em dash alone is announced as nothing, which is indistinguishable from a cell the page failed to fill.

The L1 pill is real text and its meaning is written once under the matrix. It is not aria-hidden and it is not an icon: the mark is the only thing separating one figure from three identical ones, so it has to survive being read out.

The basis control is a role="radiogroup" of role="radio" buttons with a roving tabindex, and its aria-checked is the announcement. There is no live region over the matrix: a basis change rewrites every figure in the foot, and a live region announcing all of them makes a control nobody presses twice.

The award summary is an <output> so it is a live region by default and the restatement is heard as it changes. The reason field is an ordinary labelled textarea with its message paragraph, and the button that needs it is guarded rather than disabled, so it keeps focus and can say why it refused.

The terms band is part of the same table with its own <tbody> and a <th scope="colgroup"> naming it, not a second table below. Split into two tables the vendor columns lose their headers in the second one, and a payment term is announced with no vendor attached to it.
